subject: Model comparison scanone, stepwise and MQM differ

messages.author: 337924c21509e64a
messages.subject: Model comparison scanone, stepwise and MQM differ
parts:
Hi everyone,

As a relative new user of R-qtl, I found this page very useful. With respect to my own research, I have some trouble in trusting the obtained data.
I'm trying to detect QTLs for a type of abiotic stress tolerance in tomato.
Because phenotyping is a major bottleneck in this research, I have only 96 individuals and 126 markers, which might become though to do QTL on.

So far, I've performed scanone, stepwise and mqmscan analysis on the data. 
From the  scanone output I did find some insignificant "peaks",  (1000 permutations)
Using the stepwise function, I do find a model with interacting QTLs (1000 permutations), corresponding to the peaks obtained in the scanone function (see script below). Remarkable, is that I only find a model when I increase the max number of QTLs. If this is lower then 12, no model is detected. 
Using mqmscan, the peaks found in scanone do overlap and become significant (1000 permutations), but using mqmgetmodel, I do not get a model.

Therefore, I am confused and highly doubt my output. Am I overlooking something or is such output trustworthy?

Any comment is much appreciated,

Kind regards,

Nicky


STEPWISE
simv7<-sim.geno(d5v7nmkos)
perms1000imp<-scantwo(simv7, method="imp", pheno.col=13, n.perm=1000)
penal1000<-calc.penalties(perms1000imp, alpha=0.05)

step7_15p<-stepwiseqtl(simv7, pheno.col=13, max.qtl=15, penalties=penal1000, 
                       keeptrace=TRUE, keeplodprofile=TRUE)

MQM

set2<-mqmsetcofactors(augv7minprob0.01, each=20)

                           cofactor.significance=0.001)
> mqmgetmodel(mqmv7set3_13)
NULL

messages.author: 6f0e81f2684a02bb
messages.subject: Re: Model comparison scanone, stepwise and MQM differ
parts:
I have not encountered not obtaining a model from stepwiseqtl(), but here are a couple of things I would check:

(a) See if your (main, heavy, and light) penalties from your two-dimensional scan for stepwiseqtl() analyses are in or near the same range as the penalties for mouse intercross from Manichaikul et al. (2009)  (3.52, 4.28, 2.69). Your penalties won't be the same, but in my experience with plant phenotypes from a biparental cross (using 24k permutations), penalties hover near or two-fold larger than these values. Perhaps increasing scantwo() permutations or trying default penalties will yield a model with less than 12 QTL.

(b) Initialize the stepwiseqtl() with the QTL model from your scanone analysis. For example, if you saw a QTL on chromosome N at position A and another QTL on chromosome M at position B:
     init_qtl <- makeqtl(inputcross, chr=c(N,M), pos=c(A,B))
     stepout <- stepwiseqtl(inputcross, pheno.col=phenotype, qtl=init_qtl, formula=y~Q1+Q2, ....)

Finally, if you're looking for a model with few false-positives, I like to follow the Manichaikul et al (2009) procedure in selecting a model based on penalties after performing stepwiseqtl() and not just the model with largest pLOD.

Sandra Truong
